analysis.one_liner: Ends the consumer financial watchdog's independent Federal Reserve funding and makes Congress approve its budget yearly.
analysis.headline: The bill had 35 Republican sponsors and was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never gave it a markup or floor vote, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, created after the 2008 financial crisis, is funded by automatic transfers from the Federal Reserve rather than by the annual spending process, so Congress cannot use its budget to pressure it. The TABS Act would have ended that independent funding and required the bureau to get its money through annual appropriations votes. Its supporters called this an accountability fix; its practical effect would have been to give banking-industry allies in Congress a yearly chokepoint to shrink or defund the agency that polices their conduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, credit bureaus, and other financial firms that the CFPB regulates would gain, because annual appropriations would give their allies in Congress a recurring opportunity to cut the bureau's budget or threaten it with shutdown unless enforcement eased. Members of Congress who want leverage over the bureau would also gain direct control of its purse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and other regulated financial firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the provisions of the Dodd-Frank-era law that fund the CFPB through transfers of Federal Reserve earnings and replaces them with an authorization subject to annual appropriations for fiscal years 2018 and 2019.
The CRS summary states that under current law the CFPB is funded outside the annual appropriations process and that the bill would bring it into the regular process.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers of financial products. If Congress could squeeze the bureau's budget every year, the agency would have less capacity to investigate deceptive lending, unfair fees, debt-collection abuse, and fraud, and the people those rules protect would bear the cost through whatever abuses returned. The Treasury would also lose the Fed-funded bureau's budget stream, meaning taxpayers would cover the agency's cost if it stayed funded.

drawbacks.text: Moving CFPB funding into annual appropriations would put the budget of the one agency that polices banks, payday lenders, and debt collectors up for yearly votes in which the industries it regulates are among the most active lobbyers, creating standing leverage to weaken enforcement without changing any law.

Supporters' accountability argument has a real basis: an agency funded automatically by Federal Reserve earnings answers to no one's purse, and bringing it into the regular process is the standard constitutional arrangement for federal agencies. The honest trade-off is between ordinary budget accountability and insulating a consumer regulator from the industry it regulates.

The authorization was limited to fiscal years 2018 and 2019 with no dedicated amount, so even under the bill's own terms the bureau's future funding level would rest entirely on yearly congressional decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is genuine in principle, but in this specific case the mechanism matters: the CFPB was deliberately placed outside appropriations so that the industries it regulates could not use the budget process against it. Making its funding subject to annual votes would not add much real oversight beyond the bureau's existing director accountability, reporting, and audits, but it would hand regulated industries a recurring pressure point. The costs to consumers outweigh the procedural benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it never received a vote in the House or the Senate and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr introduced the bill on May 19, 2017, joined by 15 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
A total of 34 Republicans cosponsored the bill, and no Democrats did.

The only recorded action after the committee referral was the referral itself; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no committee report, and no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The CFPB kept its independent funding stream, so the consumers the bureau protects came out ahead, while the bill's failure left members of Congress and the financial firms they oversee without the budget leverage the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The consumer watchdog and the people it protects

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to move CFPB funding into the annual appropriations process.

for.name: 34 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 34 recorded cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no markup, vote, or report ever followed, letting the bill expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Consumer and public-interest groups
against.role: Defenders of the CFPB's independent funding structure
against.what_they_did: Publicly defended the bureau's Federal Reserve funding as protection against industry pressure through Congress during the periodic push to change it.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans and no Democrats signed on, so the bill's support was entirely from one party; it then died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Banks, payday lenders, and consumer financial firms regulated by the CFPB
industries.note: These firms would gain a yearly congressional chokepoint over the budget of the agency that polices their lending, fee, and debt-collection practices. Their gain would come at the cost of weaker enforcement for the consumers those rules protect.

industries.industry: The consumer financial protection regime (the CFPB itself)
industries.note: The bill would end the bureau's funding independence, the design feature meant to keep its enforcement insulated from the industries it regulates, and subject its budget to annual congressional votes. Its loss of independence would mean less consistent protection for ordinary consumers.
